q: Which element forms at the cathode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
explain: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions from the water are discharged at the cathode instead.

q: Which electrolyte should be used to silver-plate a ring?
options: A solution containing silver ions, such as silver nitrate
explain: The electrolyte for plating must contain ions of the plating metal so that they can be discharged at the cathode.

q: Which solution is not an electrolyte?
explain: Glucose is a covalent molecule and gives no ions in water. The other solutions contain mobile ions.

q: In which electrolysis would a gas that relights a glowing splint form at the anode?
options: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride with inert electrodes
Dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes
Molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes
Molten zinc chloride with inert electrodes
explain: Only dilute sulfuric acid gives oxygen at the anode. The other electrolytes give halogens.

q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Chlorine at the cathode and sodium at the anode
explain: There is no water in the molten compound, so the only ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

q: How can an iron nail be electroplated with zinc?
options: Use the nail as the anode and zinc as the cathode in a solution of a zinc salt
Use the nail as the cathode and graphite as the anode in distilled water
Heat the nail in molten zinc and pass a current through it
Use the nail as the cathode and zinc as the anode in a solution of a zinc salt
explain: The object to be plated is made the cathode and the anode is the plating metal. The electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal.

q: Which statement about electroplating is correct?
options: A thin layer of metal is deposited on the anode
A thin layer of metal is deposited on the cathode
The object being plated is made the positive electrode
The electrolyte must be a molten non-metal
explain: Positive metal ions are attracted to the negative cathode, which is the object being plated.

q: Which substance is the fuel in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
explain: Hydrogen is the substance that is oxidised, so it is the fuel. Oxygen is the other reactant, and water is the product.

q: Where does a hydrogen fuel cell car usually get its oxygen from?
options: The decomposition of water in the engine
explain: Air contains about 21% oxygen, so there is no need for the car to carry oxygen.

q: What is the electricity from a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell used for in a fuel cell car?
options: To burn hydrogen in a cylinder
explain: The cell produces electricity, which drives an electric motor to move the vehicle.

q: Why should the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide be done in a fume cupboard?
options: The electrodes give off carbon dioxide
explain: Bromine is a poisonous red-brown vapour, so it must be removed safely.

q: Which metal forms at the cathode when molten magnesium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes?
explain: Mg²⁺ ions are positive, so they move to the cathode and become magnesium atoms.

q: Which row correctly describes the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes?
explain: Bromine is a non-metal and forms at the anode as red-brown fumes. Lead forms at the cathode.

q: During the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid, 20 cm³ of oxygen is collected at the anode. What volume of hydrogen forms at the cathode, measured under the same conditions?
explain: The ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2 : 1 (2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂), so hydrogen is 2 × 20 = 40 cm³.

q: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, which ion moves towards the anode?
explain: The anode is positive and attracts negative ions, which are the bromide ions.

q: Which half-equation shows oxidation?
explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Only the chloride half-equation has electrons on the product side.

q: Which half-equation shows reduction?
explain: Reduction is gain of electrons, so the electrons appear on the left-hand side, as in Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag.

q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the cathode in the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride?
explain: Each Na⁺ ion gains one electron. The other equations are not balanced for charge or have electrons on the wrong side.

q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the anode in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide?
explain: Two oxide ions form one O₂ molecule and release 4 electrons. Check charge: −4 on the left and −4 on the right.

q: Concentrated aqueous potassium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
explain: Hydrogen ions are discharged at the cathode because hydrogen is less reactive than potassium. In a concentrated halide solution, iodine forms at the anode.

q: Why is hydrogen, not sodium, formed at the cathode when aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed?
options: Hydrogen is less reactive than sodium, so H⁺ ions are discharged more easily
Sodium is less reactive than hydrogen, so Na⁺ ions are discharged more easily
Sodium reacts with chlorine as soon as it forms
Sodium ions are not present in the solution
explain: In aqueous solutions, the less reactive element is discharged at the cathode. Hydrogen is below sodium in the reactivity series.

q: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Copper at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
explain: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ is discharged at the cathode. Cl⁻ is discharged at the anode in a concentrated solution.

q: What happens to the acidity of aqueous copper(II) sulfate during electrolysis with carbon electrodes?
options: It becomes more acidic because H⁺ ions are left in the solution
It becomes more alkaline because OH⁻ ions are left in the solution
It stays neutral because only copper is removed
It becomes more acidic because SO₄²⁻ ions are removed
explain: OH⁻ ions are removed as oxygen at the anode, leaving H⁺ ions with the sulfate ions, so sulfuric acid forms.

q: Which pair of half-equations shows the reactions in aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon electrodes?
options: Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; anode: 2OH⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + 2e⁻
explain: Copper ions are reduced at the cathode and hydroxide ions oxidised at the anode. The final option is not balanced (two OH⁻ cannot give H₂O and O₂).

q: How many moles of electrons are needed to deposit 0.25 mol of copper from aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
explain: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 mol of electrons per mole of copper, so 0.25 × 2 = 0.50 mol.

q: 1.28 g of copper is deposited at the cathode. The relative atomic mass of copper is 64. How many moles of electrons were transferred?
explain: Moles of Cu = 1.28 ÷ 64 = 0.020 mol. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu so electrons = 2 × 0.020 = 0.040 mol.

q: In the electrolytic purification of copper, which happens at the impure copper anode?
explain: The copper anode takes part, losing electrons to form Cu²⁺ ions. Pure copper is deposited on the cathode.

q: A steel spoon is silver-plated in silver nitrate solution. What reaction occurs at the spoon?
explain: The spoon is the cathode, where silver ions gain electrons (reduction) and form silver metal.

q: A nickel anode is used to nickel-plate an object. Which pair of half-equations describes the changes?
options: Anode: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni; cathode: Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻
Anode: Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni
explain: Nickel metal is oxidised at the anode and nickel ions are reduced at the cathode, so the concentration of nickel ions stays constant.

q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell car compared with a petrol car?
options: Hydrogen is easier to store and transport than petrol
The only waste product is water, so no carbon dioxide is released during use
There are more refuelling stations for hydrogen
The fuel cell never needs oxygen
explain: Petrol burning releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. The fuel cell forms only water.
